strengths: The core idea is clean and well-motivated: modeling trajectory-level verifiable rewards as a sum of token log-probabilities of a small module (Eq. 4) yields an additive, backbone-agnostic guidance signal (Eq. 5), with a sensible derivation from the KL-regularized RL optimal policy form (Eqs. 1-3).

The plug-and-play guidance module is genuinely architecture-agnostic (logit-level combination), which is a meaningful practical contrast to LoRA adapters tied to a specific backbone, and enables the weak-to-strong transfer and composition experiments.

Evaluation is relatively broad: two model families (Llama3.2, Qwen2.5), two task types (math reasoning with five benchmarks; machine translation), transferability to 8B/14B frozen backbones, a module-size ablation (0.5B vs 1.5B), a VLM extension (Appendix C.1), and VRAM/efficiency measurements.
The naive logit-sum ablation (Baseline + 1B / + 0.5B degrading below baseline) is a valuable control showing reward-driven training of the module, not mere ensembling, drives the gains.

The paper is honest about negative results (UniR does not surpass GRPO on Qwen2.5) and includes an explicit Limitations section; the appendix provides prompts, hyperparameters, and reward implementations, supporting reproducibility.
The training dynamics analysis (Section 5.5) connecting low reward variance in UniR to GRPO advantage normalization and the difficulty bias from Dr.GRPO is an interesting empirical observation.
weaknesses: The theoretical contribution is weak. Theorem 1 is informal and its proof is essentially circular: it assumes the guided policy converges to the optimal policy and that Eq. (4) holds, then deduces log pi_r = Q*/beta. Nothing establishes when or whether Eq. (4) is satisfied by a module trained with GRPO, and there is no empirical validation of the reward-likelihood fit. The claim of 'theoretical justification' is therefore overstated.

The central claim that UniR 'significantly outperforms existing baseline fine-tuning methods' is only half-supported: on Qwen2.5, UniR (42.2 avg) is below both GRPO Full (44.8) and GRPO LoRA (42.8); the headline win occurs only with Llama3.2. The abstract and contributions overstate the empirical picture.

The most closely related method, GenARM [40], is discussed but never compared against experimentally. The delta over GenARM (training the guidance module with GRPO on predefined rewards rather than fitting a reward model to preferences) is the paper's main novelty, and a direct comparison is needed to substantiate it. Other token-level guidance baselines (FUDGE/PECT-style, value-based sampling) are also absent.

Statistical rigor is lacking: single runs, no seeds, no variance or significance tests. Several reported differences are within noise, especially AIME24 where 30 problems make a 6.7-point gap one question (e.g., GRPO Full 3.3 vs UniR 16.7), and the transfer gains (35.5 vs 33.7; 52.8 vs 51.1) are modest.
There is a potential confound in the baseline comparison: UniR sets beta_KL = 0 while GRPO baselines use beta = 0.04, and the ablation with beta_KL = 0 for the GRPO baselines is not reported.

The composability experiment (Section 5.3) is a single constructed task (German math translated to English) judged by GPT-4.1-nano; while illustrative, it does not establish composability as a general capability, and the 'optimal composition' claim in the contributions is not backed by any optimality analysis.
Fixed inference-time overhead of an extra module forward pass is acknowledged but not quantified against alternative test-time-compute baselines (e.g., Best-of-N) at matched compute.

Presentation issues: the abstract's 'Code is open-sourced at' sentence is truncated with no URL; several grammatical errors (e.g., 'Composibility', 'requires retraining'); Figure 4 is nearly illegible at its printed size; the paper sometimes conflates 'reasoning module' quality claims with anecdotal single examples (Figures 3, 12, 15) rather than systematic analysis.

strengths: The core idea—training a small, independently-learned reasoning policy and adding its logits to a frozen backbone at inference—is clean, well-motivated, and aligned with practical needs for modularity and resource efficiency.

The paper is generally well-organized, with a clear problem formulation connecting trajectory-level verifiable rewards to token-level guidance, and covers a reasonable set of benchmarks (GSM8K, MATH-500, AIME24, Minerva, OlympiadBench; IWSLT translation with BLEU/CometKiwi/XComet).
Useful supplementary analyses: VRAM/batch-size scaling (Fig. 5), reward-variance dynamics vs. GRPO (Fig. 6), reasoning-module size ablation (Table 5), and an extension to VLM backbones (Table 4).
Honest limitations section acknowledging dependence on the backbone's capabilities and inference-time overhead.
Hyperparameters, prompts, and reward configurations are documented in sufficient detail in the appendix, aiding reproducibility.
weaknesses: Overstated central claim: the abstract asserts UniR 'significantly outperforms existing baseline fine-tuning methods,' but on Qwen2.5 the full GRPO baseline outperforms UniR (44.8 vs. 42.2 avg. in Table 1). The strong result holds only for the Llama3.2 family, and the body text admits this discrepancy while the abstract does not.

Missing the most relevant baseline: GenARM [40] is explicitly cited as providing token-level reward-model guidance over a frozen LLM, yet it (and other guided-decoding methods such as value-guided decoding or BoN at matched inference compute) is not compared against. Without this comparison, it is impossible to determine how much of the gain comes from GRPO-style reward optimization of the guide vs. simply additive logit guidance.

The theoretical contribution is weak. Theorem 1's 'proof' is circular: it assumes πθ has already converged to the optimal KL-regularized policy (itself the claim to be justified) and asserts uniqueness of the optimum without proof. Moreover, Eq. (4) posits reward as summed log-probabilities of πr, but πr is trained with GRPO to maximize r, not to satisfy Eq. (4); the paper never establishes that the trained module actually satisfies this identity.

The 'universal' and transferability claims are narrower than stated. Logit addition requires a shared vocabulary/tokenizer, so cross-family transfer (e.g., a Qwen module guiding a Llama backbone) is neither tested nor discussed; all transfers are within-family. The measured weak-to-strong gains are also small (35.5 vs. 33.7 for 8B; 52.8 vs. 51.1 for 14B) with no variance estimates, seeds, or statistical significance testing anywhere in the paper.

The composability experiment (Sec. 5.3, Fig. 4) is a single synthetic task evaluated by GPT-4.1-nano as judge, without human validation of the judge or comparison against simpler alternatives; the strong composability claims in the abstract rest on this thin evidence.

Novelty over GenARM and related guided-generation work is incremental: the main delta is training the guide via policy gradient on verifiable rewards rather than from preference data. The paper would benefit from a sharper articulation of why this distinction matters empirically.

Inference overhead of running πr alongside πb at every decoding step is acknowledged in limitations but never quantified (latency/throughput numbers are absent), which is important for judging the practical trade-off against a single fine-tuned 3B model.

Presentation issues reduce polish: 'Code is open-sourced at' ends the abstract with no link; several grammatical problems ('Composibility', 'typically requires retraining', 'amplified signals mode effectively'); Eq. (5)'s partition-function handling and the interaction between decoding temperature and additive guidance are under-specified.

strengths: The core idea is clean and practical: decouple reasoning capability into a small, self-contained module trained with GRPO on verifiable rewards, then apply it to any frozen LLM via logit addition. This sidesteps architecture-dependency of LoRA/PEFT and enables test-time composition without retraining.

The evaluation covers several complementary angles: two task families (math reasoning, machine translation), transferability to larger backbones (8B, 14B), module-size ablations (0.5B vs 1.5B), a naive logit-ensemble control ('Baseline + 1B') that usefully shows reward-driven alignment matters beyond mere ensembling, memory-efficiency measurements, training-dynamics analysis, and even a VLM extension.

The paper is transparent where results are mixed: it explicitly reports that UniR does not surpass GRPO on Qwen2.5 and instead frames the gain relative to the naive logit-sum baseline. The limitations section is honest about the frozen-backbone ceiling and inference overhead.

Reproducibility support is good: detailed hyperparameter tables, prompt templates, reward formulations, and evaluation protocols (including LLM-judge prompts) are provided, and code is stated to be open-sourced.

The framing that the composition of multiple specialized modules (math + translation) enables multi-objective control at inference time (Figure 4, Figure 14) is an interesting and practically valuable demonstration of the additive logit structure.
weaknesses: Theoretical justification is weak. Equation (4) posits (1/beta) r(x,y) = sum_t log pi_r(y_t|x,y_<t), but the module is trained to maximize r(x,y) directly via GRPO, not to satisfy Eq. (4). Theorem 1 is labeled 'informal' and its proof is circular: it assumes (i) the guided policy has converged to the optimum and (ii) Eq. (4) holds, then concludes log pi_r = Q*/beta. This does not establish that GRPO-trained pi_r approximates the soft Q-function, so the Q*-interpretation is more of a heuristic than a guarantee.

The central performance claim is overstated relative to the evidence. The abstract and contributions claim UniR 'significantly outperforms existing baseline fine-tuning methods,' yet on Qwen2.5 (Table 1) GRPO Full clearly beats UniR (44.8 vs 42.2 avg), and GRPO LoRA beats it too (42.8 vs 42.2). Only the Llama3.2 setting supports superiority, and transfer gains to 8B/14B backbones are modest (+1.8 and +1.7 average points).

Missing comparison with the most relevant baseline. GenARM [40] — cited as closely related token-level reward-guided decoding for frozen LLMs — is not empirically compared against. Nor are other guided-decoding methods (value-augmented sampling, PPLM/FUDGE-style token guidance, contrastive decoding variants), which would clarify UniR's added value over existing test-time guidance approaches.

No statistical rigor: all results appear to be single runs with no error bars, seeds, or significance tests. AIME24 has only 30 problems, where a single flip changes the score by ~3.3 points, making some reported differences (e.g., 16.7 vs 13.3 vs 10.0) unreliable.

The 'Universal' framing is limited in scope. Transferability is only demonstrated within the same model family (Qwen2.5-0.5B to Qwen2.5-14B, Llama3.2-1B to Llama3.1-8B). Since logit addition requires a shared vocabulary/tokenizer, true cross-family or cross-architecture transfer — the property that would distinguish this from LoRA — is never shown. The paper's criticism of LoRA's 'model dependency' is only partially addressed.

The compositional experiment relies on GPT-4.1-nano as the judge for both translation quality and math accuracy, which is a noisy and potentially biased evaluation protocol; no human validation of the judge is provided.

Section 5.5's stability argument (lower reward variance amplifies advantage magnitudes, which is claimed as beneficial) is speculative and partially contradicts the cited 'difficulty bias' concern in [24]; the reasoning here would benefit from formal or at least controlled empirical analysis.

strengths: The core idea is well-motivated and cleanly presented: a small reasoning module trained with GRPO on verifiable rewards, added to a frozen backbone at the logit level. The additive composition is grounded in the standard KL-regularized multi-objective alignment framework rather than presented as a heuristic (Eq. 5–6).

Unusually comprehensive empirical evaluation for this area: five math benchmarks plus machine translation (Table 1–2), transferability to 8B/14B backbones (Fig. 2), a compositional German-math task (Fig. 3), VLM transfer, MIMIC-IV medical tasks, low-resource languages, pre-trained-module reuse (Table 18), cross-tokenizer transfer (Table 10), and comparisons against the closest methods (Reasoning Vectors, RAST in Table 11).

Good experimental hygiene: pass@1 reported over 10 seeds with standard deviations, an explicit analysis of greedy vs. stochastic decoding (Tables 16–17) that explains discrepancies with reported baselines and supports the mode-collapse argument, ablations on module size (Table 15), VRAM/throughput analysis (Fig. 6, Table 12), gradient-norm stability analysis (Table 13), and failure-case analysis (J.5).

Honest limitations discussion (Appendix C) covering backbone-bounded performance, potential negative interference under conflicting rewards, and tokenizer mismatch, plus an appropriate impact statement for the medical experiments.
weaknesses: Limited methodological novelty relative to prior work. The core mechanism (token-level logit addition of a smaller guiding model to a frozen backbone) is essentially GenARM (Xu et al., 2024b), and the central theory (Lemma A.1) is explicitly imported from that paper (Theorem 3). The paper's framing acknowledges this, but the delta is primarily 'use verifiable rewards + GRPO instead of a preference-trained reward model,' which is a reasonable but incremental distinction over GenARM/RAST/MT-based guidance.

Theorem 4.1 is close to circular: it assumes πθ converges to the optimal policy and then reads off that log πr equals the scaled soft Q*. It provides little insight into whether or when the proposed training actually converges there; the 'Empirical Validation' (Fig. 5) shows correct responses score higher, which is a weak, largely pre-existing effect ('before training' separation is already present).

Baseline fairness concerns: (i) the KL coefficient differs between methods (βKL=0 for UniR vs. β=0.04 for GRPO baselines), a confound that is justified but not ablated for the baselines; (ii) the headline comparisons (e.g., 'Ours 1.5B' vs. 'GRPO Full 3B') involve a guided policy that effectively combines 3B+1.5B parameters at inference vs. a single 3B model, and the memory argument in App. F is about training only. The efficiency advantage is real for training but partially eroded at inference, as the authors themselves concede (Table 6, naive UniR is ~58% slower).

Results on the hardest benchmark are mixed: AIME24 is inconsistent (e.g., UniR 7B underperforms GRPO Full 7B by 2.5 points in Table 9), and gains on OOD benchmarks are moderate relative to the strong Qwen GRPO baselines. The medical composability results show accuracy degradation when modules are combined (Table 3), which weakens the composability claim in that domain.
Evaluation of the compositional German-math task relies on GPT-4.1-nano as judge for both translation quality and correctness, with limited validation of the judge's reliability.

Reproducibility is hampered by an incomplete code link (the abstract's URL is truncated/missing), although hyperparameters, prompts, and reward configurations are otherwise documented in detail (Tables 7–8, Appendix I).

strengths: Comprehensive empirical evaluation across many tasks (math reasoning, machine translation, VLM, medical, low-resource languages) with ablations on module size, decoding temperature, and comparisons to closely related guidance methods (RAST, Reasoning Vectors, GenARM context)

Practical efficiency story is well supported: memory/batch-size analysis (Fig. 6), training throughput, gradient-norm stability analysis (Table 13), and inference-overhead mitigation via speculative decoding (Table 6)
The paper is generally well written, with detailed hyperparameters, prompt templates, limitations discussion (Appendix C), and an honest impact statement regarding medical experiments
Honest reporting of negative results in places, e.g., cross-tokenizer transfer degrades performance (Table 10) and module composition reduces accuracy in the medical setting (Table 3)
weaknesses: Limited novelty relative to prior work: logit-level guidance of a frozen large model by a small auxiliary model is already established by GenARM (Xu et al., 2024b) and RAST (Ouyang et al., 2025); the main delta is replacing a preference-based reward model with verifiable rewards, and Lemma A.1 is explicitly restated as 'Theorem 3 in Xu et al. (2024b)'. The theoretical contribution is thus largely a re-derivation adapted to a new reward source

The composability claim is mathematically trivial: weighted logit addition is the standard solution to KL-regularized multi-objective alignment, as the authors themselves note; the empirical composition results are narrow (one German-math task) and the medical composition actually degrades accuracy versus single modules, weakening the headline 'composable' contribution

Theorem 4.1 assumes convergence to the optimal policy, which is unverifiable; the 'empirical validation' (correct responses get higher summed log-probabilities, Fig. 5) is a weak test that could equally be explained by the module learning superficial answer-format signals rather than approximating a soft Q-function

Fairness of comparisons is questionable: UniR deploys backbone + auxiliary module (e.g., 3B + 1.5B, more total parameters and 1.6x inference time) against GRPO fine-tuning of the 3B alone; the abstract's claim of surpassing fine-tuning methods is not consistently supported — under greedy decoding (Table 16) GRPO Full slightly outperforms UniR on Qwen (44.8 vs 43.9), and on the 7B backbone (Table 9) GRPO Full wins on AIME24 and OlympiadBench, with only a marginal overall gap

The 'robustness to decoding temperature' framing appears constructed to favor the method: gains over baselines at T=0.6 largely vanish at T=0, and the claim that GRPO baselines suffer mode collapse is asserted but not deeply analyzed

The 'universal' branding is overstated given the results: cross-tokenizer transfer yields 18.3 vs. a 35.6 backbone-only baseline (Table 10), and cross-family transfer requires vocabulary alignment machinery not contributed by this paper

Several secondary results are weak or thinly analyzed: the readmission F1 gain is +0.9 points, the low-resource language and composition evaluations rely on GPT-4.1-nano as judge without validation, and the interpretive narrative around Fig. 3 (translation module improving math accuracy) is speculative

Baseline strength is uncertain: all GRPO baselines use only 1000 steps with a fixed learning rate and identical hyperparameters across methods; no evidence is provided that the GRPO baselines were tuned to their potential, which is essential given the central claim of outperforming standard RFT

strengths: Clear, well-motivated idea: decoupling reasoning into a small trainable module that provides token-level logit guidance to a frozen backbone, enabling plug-and-play transfer, composability, and efficiency gains

Comprehensive experimental coverage: math reasoning (5 benchmarks), machine translation, transferability to 7B/8B/14B backbones, module composition, VLM extension, medical tasks, low-resource languages, and inference-speed mitigation via speculative decoding

Useful analysis of why the method works: reward decomposition validation (Fig. 5), training stability and gradient norm analysis (Table 13, Fig. 7), and demonstration that the module is not merely a stronger standalone model (Table 14)
Direct comparison with the most relevant concurrent guidance methods (Reasoning Vectors, RAST in Table 11), including a cross-tokenizer evaluation and honest discussion of its limitations
Good reproducibility: full hyperparameter tables, prompt templates, reward implementations, standard deviations over 10 seeds, open-sourced code, and an LLM-usage declaration
Honest limitations section and appropriate ethical treatment of MIMIC-IV data and clinical-deployment caveats
weaknesses: Limited theoretical novelty: Lemma A.1 is explicitly restated from Xu et al. (2024b), and Theorem 4.1's proof is essentially substituting definitions under an assumed convergence to the optimal policy; the bridge between the trajectory-level distribution πr in Lemma A.1 and an actual autoregressive LM over a shared token space (conditioning structure, expressivity) is argued loosely

Incremental novelty over prior plug-and-play guidance work: GenARM already uses additive token-level guidance from a smaller autoregressive model, and RAST uses logit-space transfer; the core differentiator (verifiable-reward training of the guide) is an empirical rather than conceptual advance

Some evidential gaps in headline claims: at T=0 the margin over GRPO LoRA/Full with Qwen shrinks to ~1 point (Tables 16/17), the 7B-scale comparison is mixed (GRPO Full wins on AIME24 and OlympiadBench, Table 9), and the composition result where a translation module improves math accuracy is explained post-hoc rather than predicted by the framework

Training configurations are not identical across methods (e.g., βKL=0 for UniR but β=0.04 for baselines), and baseline hyperparameters appear to follow defaults rather than per-method tuning, which could contribute to the observed performance gaps and instability of GRPO baselines

Medical results are oddly framed: composition reduces accuracy on the constituent tasks (Table 3), the LOS baseline of 9.64% accuracy suggests a near-random baseline, and gains on the unseen mortality task lack statistical rigor

Composability claim is demonstrated on only one composite task with LLM-judged evaluation (GPT-4.1-nano), and the negative-interference phenomenon acknowledged in the limitations is not systematically analyzed
Presentation issues: duplicated references (Su et al. 2025a/b), minor grammatical errors, and the distinction between this work and GenARM beyond the reward source could be stated more crisply
